lesson.grammar_point: second conditional for hypothetical questions and answers: if + past simple / were, would + verb (if I were you)

listenings.text: Thank you, that was a very useful presentation. I've got three quick questions, if that's all right. First, before we placed any order, we would need the full spec sheet, with the alloy and the thickness of every product. Could you send that? Second, volume. If we doubled our order next year, could your company scale up in time, or would the lead time get longer? And third, the price. I know it's difficult to say now, but if you could give me a ballpark figure by the end of the week, that would help a lot. I don't need the exact number today. Thanks very much.

That's a good question, and I'll be honest with you. If you ordered every month instead of every quarter, we could plan our production much better, and your lead time would go down from twelve weeks to about eight. That is the trade-off for us: regular orders, faster delivery. About the price, I'm afraid I can't give you a fixed price for two years. The price of aluminum changes every day on the market, and if we promised a fixed price, we would be taking a very big risk. What I can offer is a fixed price for six months, and then a review. If I were you, I would accept that. It's what most of our clients in Europe do.

Here's something I see all the time. People spend three weeks on their slides and three minutes thinking about the questions. And then the Q&A session starts, and that's where the deal is really made or lost. My advice? Write down the ten questions you'd hate to get, and prepare them. And if somebody asks you something you really don't know, don't invent a number. Just say: that's a great question, let me check and get back to you by Thursday. People respect that. Oh, and one more thing. When the audience starts asking what-if questions, if we did this, would you do that, relax. That's a good sign. It means they're already imagining the deal.
